Public-domain scan, archive.org dli.ernet.28761 (Digital Library of India); second scan;ernet.dli.2015.40129; third (eGangotri) scan of JASB 25(1) Aug 1929.
catalog_locator: p. 9, section 'TONE.'; vocabulary head-note on p. 55 (confirmed: 'VOCABULARY. N.B.—h.p. or l.p..' opens that page)
catalog_quote: TONE. As in all Naga languages difference of meaning depending on the tone in which a word is spoken is a fertile source of difficulty. In Chang, as in Serna [scan for Sema], three tones may be disting-uished, but the difference is very often so slight as to be indistinguishable to any but a Chang. A few instances are given, h standing for ' high ', m for ' medium ', and l for ' low ' pitch :— mttgh [scan; mügh], h = sky l = hunger. ch&m [chám], h = salt l = house. tel [tei], h = there l = water. wan, m = fire l = winnower. lang, m = stone l = horn. uwi, m = soap; nasal excretion l = fur. Likewise the difference between k&m (h) = " do " and kSmm l = " forbid " is very slight. There are also words with two meanings where there is no difference in tone, e.g :— l&ng (1) thatch, (2) rain, m&ng (1) shadow, (2) dream, ... [p. 55, head of VOCABULARY:] N.B.—h.p. or l.p. (p. = pitch) after a word indicates that the tone is high or low accordingly.

In Chang, as in Sema, three tones may be distinguished, but the difference is very often so slight as to be indistinguishable to any but a Chang. A few instances are given, h standing for 'high', m for 'medium', and l for 'low' pitch :— mügh, h = sky, l = hunger. chäm, h = salt, l = house. tei, h = there, l = water. wan, m = fire, l = winnower. lang, m = stone, l = horn. uwi, m = soap; nasal excretion, l = fur.

new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (104 pp; contents page lists 'Tone.. 9'). extracted text of PDF page 10 gives the running head '1929.] Outline of Chang Grammar. 9' followed by 'Euphony.' and then 'TONE. As in all Naga languages difference of meaning depending on the tone in which a word is spoken is a fertile source of difficulty. In Chang, as in Serna [scanned for Sema], three tones may be disting-uished, but the difference is very often so slight as to be indistinguishable to any but a Chang. A few instances are given, h standing for c high m for ' medium and l for 1 low ' pitch :- mttgh, h == skv 1 = hunger. ch&m, h = salt / = house. tel, h = there l = water. wan, m = fire / = winnower. lang, m = stone l = horn.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chang is described as a tone language with three lexically contrastive pitch levels (high, medium, low) on monosyllabic words; the source says nothing about word stress or accent placement at all (the only occurrences of 'stress'/'accent' in the 101 pages are in the vocabulary, 'Distress'). The vocabulary marks high and low pitch on words ('h.p.'/'l.p.'). No statement of a stress rule exists in this source.
new_statements.exceptions: Hutton notes that the tone differences are 'very often so slight as to be indistinguishable to any but a Chang', apologises for not marking tones systematically in the grammar, and lists homophones with no tonal difference (lang 'thatch/rain', mang 'shadow/dream', etc.). Diphthongs ou/ei in simple words 'usually become o and e in compounds unless they occur in the final syllable of the compound word' (p. 7) — a positional vowel reduction, not framed as stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms of monosyllabic lexemes; no phrase-level prosody described. The tone analysis is impressionistic (1915-17 field notes, published 1929); Chor 2011 (NTU FYP, restricted) re-analyses the system as three tonemes: high level, low level, falling (abstract only seen).
new_statements.identity_note: Hutton 1929 describes the speech of the Tuensang/Mokokchung Changs recorded 1915-17 (Hutton says the language is essentially Konyak-type, closest to the Konyak of 'Zu/Banfera' per Grierson); no dialect split is named, so it is the language-level chan1313. Chor 2011 (NTU, restricted) is a modern fieldwork sketch of the same language with a different tone analysis (high level / low level / falling) from Hutton's high / medium / low.

new_statements.quote: On the other hand, Coupe (2006b) identifies 3-tone system in Chang: low level, high level and falling. Contrastingly, a falling tone is not identified by Hutton (1929). [...] The high tone is the most widespread [...]. Low tone [...] is the second most widespread in the language. Falling tone [...] is rare [...]. High tones may be realised as mid-level tones when they precede or follow a syllable with a low tone. Similarly, low tones may be realised as mid-level tones when they precede or follow a syllable with a high tone. Mid level tones do not occur on monosyllables in isolation. The alternation in tones is due to the tone sandhi effect.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (Hutton 1929: tonal, three tones, no stress statement) and as the existing statement: Chor's full text confirms a three-way tonal contrast and says nothing about word stress. It refines only the tone inventory (two level tonemes plus a rare falling toneme, with mid level as a sandhi allotone, versus Hutton's three pitch levels) and names the syllable as tonal domain; no stress placement exists on either side to conflict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chang is described as a tone language with three tonemes (high level, low level, falling; falling rare and possibly borrowed), the syllable being the tone-bearing unit (2.1: every syllable = optional onset + rhyme, 'Tonemes are discussed in 2.4'); mid level [33] is not a toneme but a tone-sandhi realisation of H next to L and of L next to H. Nowhere in the 50 pages is word stress, accent or syllable prominence mentioned (0 hits for stress/accent/pitch/intonation; 'word prosody' is used only for the distribution of the glottal stop, p. 5). So: tone language, no stress statement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned (no stress discussion at all)
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; on tone: Hutton 1929's high/mid/low analysis is contrasted with Coupe 2006b's low/high/falling, which the author adopts; tone sandhi 'approximated' as H or L -> [33] adjacent to the opposite tone, further study deferred.
new_statements.identity_note: Chang (Chang Naga, ISO nbc) of Tuensang district, Nagaland. Chor's FYP is based on the author's own Nagaland fieldwork (800-item wordlist, 2 narratives; village not stated in the abstract); French 1983 treats Chang as one of seven Northern Naga dialects (with Yogli, Moshang, Nocte, Wancho, Wakching Konyak, Phom) from published sources (his 2.1 'Sources', p. 85, gated).

tone_statements.citation: Coupe, Alexander R. (2014). Strategies for analyzing tone languages. Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 462-489. (series 'How to Study a Tone Language', eds. S. Bird & L. Hyman)
tone_statements.quote: Chang is found to have a high /55/ toneme, a high-falling /51/ toneme, and a low /11/ toneme, as respectively represented by the blue, red and green F0 contours of Figure 1 above. However, when eliciting the word list I also heard a mid-level pitch in many polysyllabic environments. Figure 1 additionally demonstrates how the /55/ toneme is realised phonetically with a [33] allotone in the environment of a [11] tone in disyllabic words such as /loʊ⁵⁵-kǝɪ¹¹/ ‘come-decl’, /thu⁵⁵-kǝɪ¹¹/ ‘dig-decl’ and /we⁵⁵-kǝɪ¹¹/ ‘count-decl’, all of which are consistently uttered with [33-11] output tones.
tone_statements.locator: p. 466, §2 'Recording the data for tonal analysis', below Figure 1 'Tone sandhi effects in Chang disyllables'
tone_statements.summary: Three tonemes on the syllable: high 55, high-falling 51, low 11 (F0 plots); high is downstepped to [33] before a low-toned suffix; falling tone mostly on long vowels/diphthongs; no rising tone.

tone_statements.quote: Mongsen Ao and Chang both have three lexical tones whose domain is syllable, but they differ in the nature of their FO contours. Mongsen Ao has three terrace-like register tones on monosyllabic words uttered in citation, whereas Chang has high and low level tones, and a high falling tone. [...] In common with Mongsen Ao, Chang has distinctive intonation patterns overlaying and trumping the lexical tones of individual syllables in both finite and non-finite clauses.
tone_statements.locator: section 'The role of prosody in topic continuity', before and after Figure 4/5
tone_statements.summary: Three lexical tones on the syllable: high level /55/, low level /11/, high falling /51/; clause-level (non-final rising) intonation overrides lexical tone in discourse.

tone_statements.citation: Coupe, Alexander R. (2011). On core case marking patterns in two Tibeto-Burman languages of Nagaland. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 34(2): 21-48. doi:10.32655/LTBA.34.2.03 (open copy: DR-NTU hdl 10356/106897)
tone_statements.quote: Preliminary research reveals Chang to be a rather typical Tibeto-Burman language of Nagaland. It has three tones whose domain is the syllable (high-level σ⁵⁵, low-level σ¹¹ and high-falling σ⁵¹), frequent tone sandhi that manifests in word formation processes, a two-way voice onset time contrast between voiceless aspirated and voiceless unaspirated plosives (but not for the palatal affricate, which is a common lacuna for a number of languages in this group), and a relatively simple phonological inventory that appears to be typical of the Konyak languages, with the exception of a unique phonemic contrast in vowel length for some articulatory positions.
tone_statements.locator: p. 26, Section 2, first paragraph after the Chang speaker-number paragraph
tone_statements.summary: Three syllable tones: high level 55, low level 11, high falling 51; frequent tone sandhi in word formation.
